Trust in Courts, Trust in Credit?

An econometrics notebook on institutions and business lending

MBA Econometrics · Research notebook

Do firms tend to have more credit in countries where managers trust the courts to be fair? A lender may be more willing to lend when it expects a fair hearing and can enforce a contract. We use the World Bank Enterprise Surveys to check whether the countries line up that way.

163economies in the core model
0.60 ppcredit difference per 10 points more confidence, before adjustment
-0.67 ppsame comparison after allowing for bribery and firm size
-1.20 ppcomparison within the same region and survey year

Short answer. We found no clear evidence that countries where firms trust the courts more have more firms holding credit. The estimates are small, change direction when we account for other differences, and are uncertain. Start with the country examples and the simple checks below. Show reveals the R behind an exhibit. The later sections explain the methods in more detail.

1 The country comparison in plain English

1.1 Can we compare countries and court systems?

Why this data? The Enterprise Surveys ask comparable questions of firms in different economies. We use the national reply summary for the court-impartiality question and the share of firms with a loan or line of credit from the same survey wave. We flip the published doubt index so that the confidence score goes up when managers view courts more favorably. More confidence and more credit are each easier to read in the same direction. World Bank country survey data, indicator guide

What it means. The score describes opinions about the courts of an economy, as reported by eligible formal firms. Individual courts, judges, cases and loan applications are outside these aggregates. The World Bank’s separate Business Ready project collects measures such as litigation time and enforcement cost. Those answer a different question about court performance and are outside the Enterprise Surveys regression used here. World Bank Business Ready dispute-resolution methods

The credit, bribery, serious-obstacle and full-constraint columns are percentages from national survey estimates. The confidence column is a score out of 100. The lookup uses the archived study waves.

1.2 What do actual countries show?

Why compare peers? Start with countries surveyed in the same broad region and year. This lets us hold broad geography and timing fixed as we compare the pattern. For each of the four largest eligible groups from distinct regions, R selects economies near the lower and upper confidence quartiles. No credit outcome enters the selection rule.

# Show one comparable-year pair per selected region. Use the exact scores
# in calculations and round only to label the exhibit.
pair_label <- function(country, score) sprintf("%s (%.1f)", country, score)
tab(data.frame(
  Wave = court_pairs$Wave,
  "Lower confidence (score)" = pair_label(court_pairs$Lower_confidence, court_pairs$Lower_score),
  "Credit %" = court_pairs$Lower_credit,
  "Higher confidence (score)" = pair_label(court_pairs$Higher_confidence, court_pairs$Higher_score),
  "Credit %" = court_pairs$Higher_credit,
  "Credit gap (pp)" = court_pairs$Credit_difference, check.names = FALSE
), "Four same-region, same-year comparisons · credit gap is higher score minus lower score", digits = 1)

What we found. Spain scores higher than Armenia and has more firms holding credit. Trinidad and Tobago scores higher than Brazil and has fewer. The pairs point in different directions.

What it means. Court confidence and credit can move together, but the higher-confidence country can have less credit. Country stories illustrate the question. For an answer across the data, use all eligible comparisons and report their uncertainty.

1.3 Does the pattern hold across countries?

Why run the analysis this way? First group countries by their confidence score and look at average credit. Then ask what a ten-point score difference corresponds to, first on its own and then among countries with comparable observed bribery and average employment. The tighter check compares countries inside the same region and survey year. It uses groups of at least four economies and repeats the prior model on those same rows so a change can be separated from a change in sample.

# A descriptive check that does not assume the pattern is a straight line.
tab(court_quartiles[c("Group", "N", "Confidence", "Credit")],
    "Average credit across four ranked confidence groups · Q1 is lowest", digits = 1)

# The estimate and interval are in percentage points per 10 confidence points.
# The last row changes the outcome to the share of fully credit-constrained firms.
tab(plain_effects(court_effects), "How much does the outcome differ for ten points more confidence?")
How much does the outcome differ for ten points more confidence?
Comparison Economies Estimate 95% interval p
Confidence alone 163 0.60 [-1.39, 2.59] 0.552
Add bribery and firm size 163 -0.67 [-2.41, 1.07] 0.449
Same peer sample, without peer controls 144 -1.03 [-2.92, 0.85] 0.280
Compare within region and survey year 144 -1.20 [-3.09, 0.69] 0.212
Use full credit constraint as outcome 163 -0.01 [-1.27, 1.25] 0.986

What we found. The raw comparison is 0.60 percentage points more credit per ten confidence points. After allowing for bribery and firm size it is -0.67 points. The same-region, same-year result is -1.20 points, with an interval of [-3.09, 0.69]. All three intervals include zero. Looking for steps between the confidence groups also gives little evidence of an association after adjustment. Their joint test has p=p= 0.748. The alternate outcome, full credit constraint, gives an estimate close to zero.

What it means. The sign of the raw comparison is consistent with the lending story. That pattern does not hold up across the adjusted models. The intervals leave room for modest differences under those models. The evidence gives us no reliable basis for forecasting how widespread credit is from this national confidence score.

1.4 What happens when we compare a country with itself?

Why try it? Countries differ in long-standing ways. Comparing two survey waves for the same economy removes its fixed differences from the change comparison. The archived impartiality question is observed only once per economy. For this separate check we use an older question on whether courts are a major or very severe obstacle to business. We compare the latest two usable waves for economies in the main sample, with the earlier wave in 2013 or later for the main repeat-wave fit.

tab(court_time_coverage, "How often the two court measures can be compared over time", digits = 0)
How often the two court measures can be compared over time
Measure Economies Repeat economies
Court confidence 163 0
Severe court obstacle 181 147 
# One difference per economy. Positive Fewer_obstacles means a decline in the
# percentage of firms rating courts a serious obstacle.
tab(plain_effects(court_change_effects), "Change in credit per ten-point decline in the share reporting severe court obstacles")
Change in credit per ten-point decline in the share reporting severe court obstacles
Comparison Economies Estimate 95% interval p
Change in obstacles alone (earlier wave 2013+) 108 -1.16 [-4.27, 1.96] 0.464
Add changes in bribery, size and years between waves 108 -0.61 [-3.92, 2.71] 0.717
Allow older earlier waves 137 -0.05 [-2.89, 2.80] 0.974
Restrict both waves to 2016 or later 82 0.21 [-3.25, 3.68] 0.904

What we found. In 108 economies with two usable waves under the main date rule, a ten-point decline in the share of firms calling courts a serious obstacle corresponds to -0.61 points of change in credit holding after allowing for changes in bribery, firm size and the wave gap. The interval, [-3.92, 2.71], covers credit declines and gains. The other date windows also leave the direction uncertain.

What it means. The repeat waves show no clear pattern for the obstacle question. The question measures whether courts disrupt business. The national surveys can interview a changing mix of firms, and economic conditions can change between waves. This check tells us about changes in reported obstacles and credit, with those limits.

1.5 What should a manager take away?

Bribery. The basic adjusted model associates ten points more bribery with -7.06 points in credit holding. With geography, survey cohort and firm website use included, the estimate is -1.43 points and its interval includes zero. Bribery is a stronger correlate in the simpler model. The size of that association depends on what we compare.

Legal origin. The comparison by historical legal family is imprecise. It offers little guidance for a lender choosing between markets. Both the court score and the legal-origin category are broad indicators.

Decision. Before pricing a loan or recommending a reform, measure enforcement and lending directly. The useful operational questions are how long recovery takes, how much a lender recovers, who applies for credit, and where applications are declined. The survey gives a country comparison of credit already held.

2 The lending question

2.1 What would connect courts, bribery and credit?

A bank cares about whether a claim can be enforced, how long recovery takes and what can be recovered. The survey observes what firm managers say about impartiality. These views might contain information about enforcement, and they might also reflect difficult experiences, expectations or who encounters the courts. In related work, Visaria studies the staggered introduction of debt recovery tribunals in India and finds changes in delinquency and interest rates on larger loans. That design uses variation in the timing and applicability of a reform. Here we compare economy-level survey aggregates. Visaria, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics

Institutional exposureCourt perceptions and bribe requests during public transactions
→
Possible mechanismsRecovery risk, operating costs and incentives to apply for credit
→
Observed outcomeShare of firms holding a loan or line of credit
A confounding route

Income, banking development and state capacity can move both institutional indicators and credit holding. Credit conditions can also change how firms operate and what they report. The arrows above are hypotheses about mechanisms. The regression estimates how the aggregates move together.

Legal origin asks a different question from measured court perceptions. It classifies the historical origin of company law or the commercial code. Colonial history and other persistent economic differences can overlap with the classification, so a difference by origin has several possible explanations. Klerman et al., Journal of Legal Analysis

2.2 What does each row and variable represent?

The survey samples eligible establishments in formal nonagricultural sectors. The World Bank uses firm-level survey weights to report national indicators. Here one observation represents one economy at one survey wave, and OLS gives every economy the same weight. An estimated difference of five percentage points concerns the share of firms in otherwise comparable observed economies. It cannot tell us how the probability for an individual firm would change if that firm’s exposure changed. World Bank survey methodology

# Use descriptive names to keep a percentage, an index, and a dummy distinct.

CRIME9 Courts rated a major or very severe obstacle % of firms Alternative court measure
DISP2 Use of courts, arbitration, mediation or conciliation among firms reporting a dispute % within eligible group Pitch extension

DISP1 Firms reporting commercial disputes % of firms Pitch extension
FIN23 Firms classified as fully credit constrained % of firms Alternative outcome
T5 Firms with their own website % of firms Development sensitivity

FIN14 is a stock measured at the survey. It can reflect borrowing demand, approval, the duration of loans and decisions made in earlier years. GRAFT3 concerns bribe requests in specified public transactions, with refusals coded as positive in the published indicator. It gives us a measure of firms’ operating environment. The data do not tell us that a lender requested a bribe. World Bank indicator descriptions

3 Build the cross-section

3.1 Find the national row

Data360 stores one observation per indicator and dimension combination. For the same year and economy, there can be a national figure, exporter figures and figures for other subsets. These subsets can overlap. A simple mean of the published rows would silently substitute a different population for the national aggregate.

# Read dimension codes as text. The raw observations remain untouched.

# A national row has "_T" in all six relevant dimensions at once.
is_national <- Reduce("&", lapply(raw_credit[total_dimensions], function(x) {
  !is.na(x) & x == "_T"
}))

3.4 Verify the sign and reproduce the pitch

4 Explore before fitting

4.1 Distributions, units and unusual economies

Use the count, center, dispersion and range together. The mean describes the average economy. The median reflects the middle economy and is less affected by extreme values. Quartiles show how much of an apparent range is populated. Check the tails before fitting because an unusual regressor can exert leverage even when its credit share looks ordinary.

# Summaries reflect the economy-level sample; the SD is the ordinary sample SD.
distribution <- function(x) {
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  quartiles <- unname(quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75)))
  c(N = length(x), Mean = mean(x), SD = sd(x), Min = min(x), Q1 = quartiles[1],
    Median = median(x), Q3 = quartiles[2], Max = max(x))
}

5 Fit the first regression

5.1 From a population relationship to sample estimates

Let YiY_i be FIN14 in percentage points and DiD_i be court doubt in index points. A linear population regression function specifies a conditional mean

E[Yi∣Di]=α+βDi. E[Y_i \mid D_i] = \alpha + \beta D_i.

The stochastic equation is Yi=α+βDi+uiY_i=\alpha+\beta D_i+u_i. The disturbance uiu_i collects differences in economy conditions left out of the equation, survey measurement error and deviations from the conditional mean. Individual economies can lie above or below the line. The residual ûi=Yi−Ŷi\hat u_i=Y_i-\hat Y_i is the deviation from the fitted sample line. It is observable after fitting. The population disturbance is unobserved.

Classical linear regression assumptions and where they matter
Assumption Why we need it What to check here
Linear in the coefficients Defines the OLS form. Transformations such as log employment can enter as regressors. Scatterplots, residual plots, a fitted-powers test and a bounded model.
Variation and full column rank We need unique slope estimates. Exact collinearity prevents identifying separate slopes. Check the design rank. Inspect correlations and VIF for near redundancy.
Zero conditional mean, E[ui∣Xi]=0E[u_i\mid X_i]=0 With an appropriate sampling model, the equation estimates the specified conditional mean without systematic omitted shifts. National income and banking conditions are plausible omissions. No residual test can establish this assumption.
Sampling and generalization A population interpretation requires a sampling or outcome model for the observed economies. The archive contains available survey waves. Its coverage does not constitute a random draw of all economies or years.
Independent economy errors and constant conditional variance Support the classical covariance formula and efficiency result under the other assumptions. Use HC3 for uneven variance. Probe regional dependence separately because HC3 allows uneven variances across independent observations.
Normal errors conditional on the design With the other classical conditions, yields exact finite-sample t and F reference distributions. The HC3 tests use approximate references. We make no claim of exact normality in these data.

Under suitable sampling and finite moments, OLS can describe the best linear projection even when the conditional mean curves. The interpretation remains an economy-level association. Also, least squares with an intercept constrains the fitted residuals to sum to zero and to be orthogonal to included regressors. Those algebraic properties supply no evidence about whether population errors are independent of the regressors.

5.2 Compute OLS by hand and with R

The fitted coefficients minimize ∑i(Yi−α−βDi)2\sum_i (Y_i-\alpha-\beta D_i)^2. In simple regression the slope is the sample covariance of YY with DD divided by the sample variance of DD. The intercept places the line through the sample means.

β̂=∑i(Di−D‾)(Yi−Y‾)∑i(Di−D‾)2,α̂=Y‾−β̂D‾. \hat\beta=\frac{\sum_i (D_i-\bar{D})(Y_i-\bar{Y})}{\sum_i (D_i-\bar{D})^2}, \qquad \hat\alpha=\bar{Y}-\hat\beta\bar{D}. 

# Compute the estimates directly from the centered cross-products.
d <- study$BREADY_DISP3
y <- study$FIN14
b <- sum((d - mean(d)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((d - mean(d))^2)
a <- mean(y) - b * mean(d)

# Fit the same sample with R and verify agreement with the production model.
simple_fit <- lm(FIN14 ~ BREADY_DISP3, data = study, na.action = na.fail)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(c(a, b), unname(coef(simple_fit)))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(coef(simple_fit), coef(models$Simple))))
tab(data.frame(Term = c("Intercept", "Court doubt"),
               Manual = c(a, b), R = unname(coef(simple_fit))),
    "Verifying the two simple-regression coefficients", digits = 4)
Verifying the two simple-regression coefficients
Term Manual R
Intercept 38.0465 38.0465
Court doubt -0.0599 -0.0599 
old <- plot_start()
plot(d, y, pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(blue, alpha.f = 0.64), cex = 0.75,
     xlab = "Court doubt (index points)", ylab = "Credit holding (%)",
     main = "OLS minimizes squared vertical distances")
abline(simple_fit, col = burgundy, lwd = 2.45)
# Label three widely spaced observations to illustrate signed residuals.
i <- order(d)[round(quantile(seq_along(d), c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)))]
segments(d[i], fitted(simple_fit)[i], d[i], y[i], col = gold, lwd = 2)
points(d[i], y[i], pch = 19, col = gold, cex = 0.85)
text(d[i], y[i], study$economy[i], pos = 3, cex = 0.75, col = ink)

The fitted slope is -0.060 percentage points per index point. A ten-point difference in doubt corresponds to -0.60 points of fitted credit holding. The intercept is the fitted share at zero doubt, the index’s agreement endpoint. The slope is an average linear comparison over the observed range.

5.3 Read R2R^2 and adjusted R2R^2

The total sum of squares is the variation around the outcome mean, TSS=∑i(Yi−Y‾)2TSS=\sum_i (Y_i-\bar Y)^2. OLS with an intercept decomposes it into explained and residual sums of squares. R2=1−RSS/TSSR^2=1-RSS/TSS reports the fraction accounted for by the fitted line in this sample. Adding regressors on the same rows can only lower RSSRSS. Adjusted R2R^2 compares residual and total mean squares, using n−p−1n-p-1 and n−1n-1 degrees of freedom, respectively, with pp slopes.

# Compute the two fit measures explicitly and check summary.lm.
tss <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
rss <- deviance(simple_fit)
manual_r2 <- 1 - rss / tss
manual_adj <- 1 - (rss / df.residual(simple_fit)) / (tss / (length(y) - 1))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(manual_r2, summary(simple_fit)$r.squared)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(manual_adj, summary(simple_fit)$adj.r.squared)))
tab(data.frame(Total = tss, Explained = tss - rss, Residual = rss,
               R2 = manual_r2, Adjusted_R2 = manual_adj),
    "Simple-model variation and fit", digits = 4)
Simple-model variation and fit
Total Explained Residual R<U+00B2> Adjusted R2
62478.14 157.2473 62320.89 0.0025 -0.0037

Court doubt alone accounts for about 0.25% of the between-economy credit variation. The slightly negative adjusted statistic reflects the degrees-of-freedom penalty on a very small fit gain. Both measures describe in-sample fit and cannot establish a causal model.

6 Extend the model

6.1 What does “holding the other variables fixed” mean?

Add bribery incidence BiB_i and the natural log of average employment WiW_i to the same economies. WiW_i is measured in workers before transformation.

Yi=α+βDDi+βBBi+θlog⁡(Wi)+ui. Y_i=\alpha+\beta_D D_i+\beta_B B_i+\theta\log(W_i)+u_i.

βD\beta_D is a one-point court-doubt comparison at the same reported bribery and average employment. βB\beta_B holds court doubt and log employment fixed. When average employment doubles, log⁡(W)\log(W) changes by log⁡(2)\log(2) and the fitted share changes by θlog⁡(2)\theta\log(2). The firm-size control describes a difference across economies with different average employment. The unit still cannot identify an individual firm’s credit probability.

# Keeping the same row set separates changes in the specification from attrition.
core_fit <- lm(FIN14 ~ BREADY_DISP3 + GRAFT3 + log_workers, data = study,
               na.action = na.fail)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(model.frame(simple_fit)), rownames(model.frame(core_fit))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(coef(core_fit), coef(core))))
fit_overview <- model_fit[c("Model", "N", "Slopes", "R2", "Adjusted_R2")]
fit_overview[["Residual df"]] <- fit_overview$N - fit_overview$Slopes - 1
tab(fit_overview, "Specification ladder · read fit changes within the same sample", digits = 3)

On the same 163 economies, the core accounts for 21.5% of the observed variation, compared with 0.25% for the simple line. Its adjusted share is 20.0%. The gains show that the added variables account for more variation in the sample even after the fit penalty. The estimates still need tests and sensitivity checks to support an institutional interpretation.

6.1.1 See the partial slope directly

The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell result gives a visual interpretation. First remove the fitted contribution of bribery and log employment from both credit and court doubt. Then regress residual credit on residual doubt. Its slope equals the court slope in the full core model. This exercise shows how the conditional comparison is constructed.

# Residualize both variables against exactly the same controls and sample.
remaining_credit <- residuals(lm(FIN14 ~ GRAFT3 + log_workers, data = study))
remaining_doubt <- residuals(lm(BREADY_DISP3 ~ GRAFT3 + log_workers, data = study))
partial_line <- lm(remaining_credit ~ remaining_doubt)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(partial_line)[2]), unname(coef(core_fit)["BREADY_DISP3"]))))

old <- plot_start()
plot(remaining_doubt, remaining_credit, pch = 16, cex = 0.75,
     col = adjustcolor(blue, alpha.f = 0.6), xlab = "Court doubt after projecting out controls",
     ylab = "Credit holding after projecting out controls", main = "The partial court-doubt slope")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 2, col = grid_col)
abline(partial_line, col = burgundy, lwd = 2.2)

par(old)

The core court slope is 0.067. Its direction differs from the simple slope. The point estimate changes because the residualized comparison uses a different component of the same court measure. The change alone cannot establish which specification removes omitted-variable bias. Controls can alter a coefficient because they account for confounding, because they condition on a mechanism, or because of sampling noise. Uncertainty matters when both estimates are small.

6.2 Add a legal-origin dummy carefully

The archived QoG series lp_legor classifies the origin of company law or the commercial code. Use Li=1L_i=1 for documented English common law, Li=0L_i=0 for documented comparison origins and leave unavailable values missing. The primary pooled comparator includes the Socialist category. The stricter civil-code comparison retains only English, French, German and Scandinavian origins. The coding of mixed systems and the pitch’s imputation rule are sensitivity questions. QoG legal-origin definition

Both intervals span zero and also allow sizable differences. The full pitch set is informative as a specification check. Use of dispute resolution is measured in the group that reports disputes. Collateral is measured among borrowers, and lack of need is a reported reason for skipping an application. Including these measures can condition on selection or a lending mechanism. A higher adjusted R2R^2 for the pitch model on the same QoG rows can be real as a gain in fit while leaving those concerns intact.

7 Test the claims

7.1 Individual tests and economic magnitudes

For court doubt, bribery and the dummy, the two-sided null is H0:βj=0H_0:\beta_j=0 and the alternative is H1:βj≠0H_1:\beta_j\ne 0. Costly recovery and public transactions motivate negative expectations for doubt and bribery. The legal-origin hypothesis predicts a positive common-law comparison. Inference uses both tails. The t statistic is β̂j/SE(β̂j)\hat\beta_j/SE(\hat\beta_j) under the zero null. The p-value uses the reference probability of observing a statistic at least as far from zero as ours, conditional on the null and the inference assumptions. The 95% interval adds and subtracts a critical multiple of the standard error. If it spans zero, the corresponding two-sided test does not reject at 5%. It can still contain policy-relevant differences.

# A scaled contrast rescales the slope AND its standard error and interval.
# Exclude the standardized comparisons here so each row has business units.
teaching_effects <- core_effects[1:3, c("Comparison", "Estimate", "SE", "t", "df", "p", "Lower", "Upper")]
tab(teaching_effects, "Core t tests in interpretable credit-share units · HC3", digits = 3)
Core t tests in interpretable credit-share units · HC3
Comparison Estimate SE t df p Lower Upper
Court doubt, 10 points 0.670 0.881 0.760 159 0.448524 -1.071 2.411
Bribery incidence, 10 points -7.056 1.176 -6.000 159 1.29e-08 -9.379 -4.733
Average employment, doubled 6.026 1.582 3.808 159 0.000199 2.901 9.151

In the core model a ten-point rise in bribery is associated with 7.06 points lower credit holding. The interval excludes zero. For court doubt the interval includes zero and both signs. For a business interpretation of any coefficient, report the unit, what was held fixed and how large the interval is. A small p-value alone cannot rank two predictors or show that a reform would pay off.

7.2 F tests answer a different question

The classical test compares a restricted model with a less restricted model on identical rows. For example, the simple model imposes zero coefficients on bribery and log employment. The extra-sum-of-squares F statistic divides the reduction in residual variation per restriction by the full model’s residual mean square. The robust Wald version instead evaluates the restrictions with an HC3 covariance matrix. The study uses the number of restrictions and the full model’s residual degrees of freedom as approximate F references for the robust test.

# H0: bribery and log employment both have zero slopes, given court doubt.
nested <- anova(simple_fit, core_fit)
tab(data.frame(Restrictions = nested$Df[2], F = nested$F[2], p = nested[["Pr(>F)"]][2]),
    "Classical nested test · add bribery and size to the simple model", digits = 3)
Classical nested test · add bribery and size to the simple model
Restrictions F p
2 21.54 5.27e-09 
# Overall H0: all core slopes are zero.
# Institutions H0: the court and bribery slopes are zero, conditional on size.
test_rows <- subset(joint_results, Model == "Core", select = -Model)
tab(test_rows, "Overall and institutional joint tests on the core sample", digits = 3)
Overall and institutional joint tests on the core sample
Test F df1 df2 p
Overall classical 14.530 3 159 2.07e-08
Overall HC3 18.424 3 159 2.62e-10
Institutional HC3 18.170 2 159 7.82e-08

The institutional F statistic can be significant because one institutional measure carries most of the information. It provides no test that both slopes are individually different from zero. With a single restriction and the same covariance, F=t2F=t^2, so the simple-model slope provides a useful consistency check.

# Scale the effect and its interval to 10 court-doubt points.
simple_t <- linear_test(simple_fit, c(BREADY_DISP3 = 10))
single_f <- block_test(simple_fit, "BREADY_DISP3")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(simple_t["t"]^2), unname(single_f["F"]))))
tab(data.frame(Estimate_pp = unname(simple_t["Estimate"]),
               HC3_interval = interval(simple_t["Lower"], simple_t["Upper"]),
               t = unname(simple_t["t"]), F = unname(single_f["F"]), p = unname(single_f["p"])),

7.3 Do the institutional associations differ?

An index point of court doubt and a percentage point of bribery incidence are distinct units. Use one sample standard deviation of each adverse exposure to compare their signed slopes. Denote their SDs by sDs_D and sBs_B. The signed difference Δ=sDβD−sBβB\Delta=s_D\beta_D-s_B\beta_B is a single linear contrast. Test H0:Δ=0H_0:\Delta=0 against H1:Δ≠0H_1:\Delta\ne0. Its variance uses the two slope variances and their covariance.

Var⁡(Δ̂)=sD2Var⁡(β̂D)+sB2Var⁡(β̂B)−2sDsBCov⁡(β̂D,β̂B). \operatorname{Var}(\hat\Delta)=s_D^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_D) +s_B^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_B) -2s_Ds_B\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_D,\hat\beta_B). 

# Hold the sample SDs fixed and apply the joint HC3 covariance.
weights <- c(BREADY_DISP3 = sd(study$BREADY_DISP3), GRAFT3 = -sd(study$GRAFT3))
delta <- linear_test(core_fit, weights)
standardized <- core_effects[4:6, c("Comparison", "Estimate", "Lower", "Upper", "p")]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(delta["Estimate"]), standardized$Estimate[3])))
tab(standardized, "Adverse one-SD comparisons and the signed difference", digits = 3)
Adverse one-SD comparisons and the signed difference
Comparison Estimate Lower Upper p
Court doubt, one SD 1.101 -1.761 3.963 0.449
Bribery incidence, one SD -7.651 -10.170 -5.133 1.29e-08
Court minus bribery, one SD each 8.752 4.885 12.619 1.48e-05

A difference between two signed slopes is a separate question from a difference in their absolute magnitudes. For the latter, an exploratory test asks whether sBβB<−|sDβD|s_B\beta_B < -|s_D\beta_D|. This requires the court-minus-bribery contrast to be positive and the court-plus-bribery contrast to be negative. The larger one-sided p-value is 0.000368 in the core sample. Partial R2R^2 helps describe how much residual variation each predictor accounts for when added to the other terms.

tab(partial_fit, "Incremental fit from adding each predictor to the other core terms", digits = 4)
Incremental fit from adding each predictor to the other core terms
Term SD Partial R2
Court doubt 16.4420 0.0038
Bribery incidence 10.8433 0.1534
What the core model says

Bribery has the larger adverse standardized association in this specification. The court coefficient remains imprecise. The comparison is conditional on the particular measures, sample and covariates. The next checks ask how credible that description is under different assumptions.

8 Diagnose the model

8.1 Unequal error variance and the HC3 correction

Some survey aggregates are noisier than others. Credit differences across economies of similar observed characteristics can also have different spreads. The studentized Breusch–Pagan test asks whether the conditional error variance is constant versus related to the regressors in its auxiliary equation. Regress squared OLS residuals on the original covariates and compare nRaux2nR_{\mathrm{aux}}^2 with a chi-square reference with one degree of freedom per slope. This version uses a studentized statistic for the variance test. Koenker, Journal of Econometrics

# Calculate the core statistic by hand, then compare the model sequence.
auxiliary <- lm(I(residuals(core_fit)^2) ~ BREADY_DISP3 + GRAFT3 + log_workers,
                data = study)
bp_manual <- nobs(core_fit) * summary(auxiliary)$r.squared
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(bp_manual, bp$Chi_squared[bp$Model == "Core"])))
tab(bp, "Studentized Breusch–Pagan · null of constant conditional error variance", digits = 4)
Studentized Breusch–Pagan · null of constant conditional error variance
Model Chi squared df p
Core 0.7489 3 0.86164
QoG origin 0.8556 4 0.93085
Full pitch terms 16.8183 9 0.05164

The core test supplies little evidence of the variance relationship it looks for. The full pitch model is closer to a conventional threshold. Neither test proves homoskedasticity. Under conditional mean independence, unequal variance alone leaves the OLS coefficients consistent but can make classical standard errors unreliable and OLS inefficient relative to a correctly weighted estimator. The archive lacks comparable observation-level variances for defensible precision weights.

HC3 uses the squared leverage-adjusted residuals, ûi2/(1−hii)2\hat u_i^2/(1-h_{ii})^2, to estimate the covariance matrix. This preserves the OLS coefficients and re-estimates their uncertainty. A high-leverage row gets a larger adjustment for the residual shrinkage associated with fitting it. MacKinnon and White, Journal of Econometrics

# The matrix computation makes clear where leverage enters.
X <- model.matrix(core_fit)
bread <- summary(core_fit)$cov.unscaled
scores <- X * (residuals(core_fit) / (1 - hatvalues(core_fit)))
V3 <- bread %*% crossprod(scores) %*% bread
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(V3, hc3(core_fit))))

display_se <- subset(se_comparison, Model == "Core", select = -Model)
display_se$Term <- term_labels(display_se$Term)
tab(display_se, "Classical and HC3 uncertainty for the same coefficients", digits = 4)
Classical and HC3 uncertainty for the same coefficients
Term Estimate Classical SE HC3_SE Classical p HC3 p
Court doubt 0.0670 0.0864 0.0881 0.4395 0.4485
Bribery incidence -0.7056 0.1315 0.1176 2.79e-07 1.288e-08

A robust SE can be smaller or larger than a classical SE. Here HC3 changes the standard errors and test statistics while preserving the qualitative findings for the institutional slopes. The correction does not address omitted variables or correlations among economies.

8.2 Durbin–Watson and residual order

Durbin–Watson compares squared differences between adjacent residuals with the residual sum of squares.

DW=∑i=2n(ûi−ûi−1)2∑i=1nûi2. DW=\frac{\sum_{i=2}^n(\hat u_i-\hat u_{i-1})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n\hat u_i^2}.

The classical diagnostic asks whether the errors exhibit first-order dependence along a meaningful sequence. Here the null reference simulates independent normal errors with constant variance, holding the design fixed. In a cross-section, changing the order changes which residuals count as adjacent, even while the coefficients and residuals attached to individual economies stay the same.

# Reorder the SAME residuals, rather than refitting the core equation.
e <- residuals(core_fit)
by_code <- order(study$economy, method = "radix")
by_year <- order(study$year, study$economy, method = "radix")
by_region <- order(study$region, study$economy, method = "radix")
direct_dw <- vapply(list(by_code, by_year, by_region), function(i) dw_stat(e[i]), numeric(1))
dw_core <- subset(dw, Model == "Core", select = -Model)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(direct_dw, dw_core$DW)))
tab(dw_core, "Core Durbin–Watson values · same fit, three orderings", digits = 3)
Core Durbin–Watson values · same fit, three orderings
Order DW p
Economy code 1.916 0.5860
Survey year, then code 1.643 0.0248
Region, then code 1.711 0.0648

Ordering by survey year groups distinct economies of similar vintage together. It gives a smaller nominal p-value here. This observation motivates a cohort sensitivity and supplies no time-series interpretation for adjacent economy labels. Regional shocks are a more plausible dependence channel. Cohort and region controls can absorb shared differences in levels. Region-clustered uncertainty addresses a different issue by allowing error dependence within a region. The study has only a few uneven groups, so the notebook shows those standard errors as a sensitivity and keeps the reference tests conditional on economy independence.

region_display <- subset(region_se, Model == "Core", select = -Model)
region_display$Term <- term_labels(region_display$Term)
tab(region_display, "HC3 versus region-clustered CR1 standard errors", digits = 3)
HC3 versus region-clustered CR1 standard errors
Term HC3 Region CR1 Groups Min size Max size
Court doubt 0.088 0.128 7 2 45
Bribery incidence 0.118 0.172 7 2 45

8.3 Collinearity, functional form and influence

For a regressor XjX_j, its variance inflation factor is 1/(1−Rj2)1/(1-R_j^2), where Rj2R_j^2 comes from regressing it on the other predictors. VIF measures how redundant the regressor is within the design. A large value can make its partial coefficient unstable and imprecise. Pairwise correlations help identify overlaps driven by particular measures, but multiple predictors can be jointly redundant without a striking pairwise correlation.

# Rebuild the court VIF in the core using its auxiliary regression.
doubt_aux <- lm(BREADY_DISP3 ~ GRAFT3 + log_workers, data = study)
manual_vif <- 1 / (1 - summary(doubt_aux)$r.squared)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(manual_vif, unname(model_vif(core_fit)["BREADY_DISP3"]))))

vif_check <- vifs[vifs$Model %in% c("Core", "Full pitch terms"), ]
vif_check$Term <- term_labels(vif_check$Term)
tab(vif_check, "Variance inflation across the core and full pitch specifications")

old <- plot_start(c(1, 2))
plot(core_diagnostics$Fitted, core_diagnostics$Residual, pch = 16, cex = 0.65,
     col = adjustcolor(blue, alpha.f = 0.65), main = "Residuals versus fitted values",
     xlab = "Fitted credit share (%)", ylab = "Residual (pp)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = muted)
lines(lowess(core_diagnostics$Fitted, core_diagnostics$Residual), col = burgundy, lwd = 2)
plot(core_diagnostics$Leverage, core_diagnostics$Cook, pch = 16, cex = 0.65,
     col = adjustcolor(blue, alpha.f = 0.65), main = "Influence versus leverage",
     xlab = "Leverage (hat value)", ylab = "Cook's distance",
     ylim = c(0, max(core_diagnostics$Cook) * 1.23))
with(head(top_core_cook, 3), text(Leverage, Cook, labels = Economy, pos = 3, cex = 0.85))

par(old)

A curved smoother can signal mean misspecification. Funnel-like spread can suggest unequal variance. Large leverage means the covariates are unusual. Cook’s distance combines leverage with residual size to indicate how much the fitted regression may change when a row is omitted. These observations prompt sensitivity refits. Automatically deleting them would change the sample and could discard meaningful variation.

# RESET-style check: jointly test added powers of the fitted linear index.
tab(form_checks, "Fitted range and HC3 test of added fitted powers", digits = 4)
Fitted range and HC3 test of added fitted powers
Model Min fit Max fit Outside F df1 df2 p
Core -2.3424 61.4801 1 1.5012 2 157 0.22603
QoG origin -2.6078 61.4547 1 3.0695 2 122 0.05005
Full pitch terms 4.5321 65.4045 0 2.0405 2 117 0.13457

The added fitted-powers test looks for systematic nonlinear information remaining in the residuals. Its null sets the coefficients on the squared and cubed fitted index to zero. Even a comfortable p-value leaves room for misspecification. The linear core produces 1 fitted value outside the feasible 0–100 range, so it is useful to check the result with a bounded conditional mean.

9 Challenge the result

9.1 Add regional, timing and development controls

Income is a plausible omitted confounder. It can be associated with credit depth, regulatory capacity and exposure to bribe requests. It is unmeasured in the approved analytical inputs. Region and survey cohort account for some shared differences. T5, the share of firms with their own website, probes a dimension of firm digital adoption. Website adoption can also respond to institutions and credit. The comparison therefore asks how the estimates move under different conditioning choices. It cannot isolate the income channel.

               Bribery_pp = adjustments$Bribery,
               HC3_interval = interval(adjustments$Bribe_low, adjustments$Bribe_high),
               p = adjustments$Bribe_p, check.names = FALSE),
    "Credit-share comparison for ten points more bribery, across specifications", digits = 3)

The core estimate is -7.06 points. With all three adjustments it is -1.43 points, with interval [-4.14, 1.28]. Comparing two specifications answers a different question from comparing two p-values. Here both the size of the estimate and its precision change. The signed comparison between standardized court and bribery slopes also becomes imprecise under the combined adjustment.

9.2 Give the outcome and the sample another chance

Fractional logit models the conditional mean of FIN14 divided by 100 as a logistic function. Its fitted shares stay within zero and one. To compare with OLS we transform predictions back to percentage points, change one regressor, and average the prediction differences across economies. The numbers below use the pipeline’s leverage-adjusted sandwich covariance and a delta-method interval for the nonlinear prediction difference. Papke and Wooldridge, Journal of Applied Econometrics

# Reproduce the average fitted difference for a 10-point increase in bribery.
# This is a prediction contrast evaluated on the same observed economies.
shifted <- transform(study, GRAFT3 = GRAFT3 + 10)
frac_rebuilt <- 100 * mean(predict(fractional, shifted, type = "response") -
                             predict(fractional, study, type = "response"))
frac_bribe <- subset(fractional_changes, Term == "GRAFT3")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(frac_rebuilt, frac_bribe$Estimate, tolerance = 1e-8)))
tab(data.frame(Model = c("Core OLS", "Fractional logit"),
               Estimate = c(main_bribery$Estimate, frac_rebuilt),
               Lower = c(main_bribery$Lower, frac_bribe$Lower),
               Upper = c(main_bribery$Upper, frac_bribe$Upper)),
    "Linear and bounded models · credit holding per ten points more bribery")

In the narrower samples and the court-obstacle alternatives, the court intervals continue to include zero. The core bribery associations persist when the selected influential economies are left out one at a time. With FIN23, more bribery is associated with a larger fully credit-constrained share. FIN23 classifies firms using financing sources and application or nonapplication information. Read the sign as more constraint in that distinct outcome. The supplemental regressions are diagnostic comparisons. Their intervals are pointwise and the reported p-values carry no multiple-comparisons adjustment.

10 Draw conclusions from the chain of evidence

The raw survey rows determine which firms and waves the study describes. The simple model asks whether court doubt alone explains much of the difference in credit holding. The core model compares economies with similar reported bribery exposure and firm size, and the legal-origin extension compares documented historical categories. The diagnostics show why HC3 and bounded-response checks are worthwhile. The sensitivity to geography and digital adoption changes the strength of the substantive conclusion.

Court perceptions

The point estimate changes sign after adding controls. The intervals still admit both signs. We learn that the measured perception indicator provides little precise evidence about credit holding in these specifications.

Bribery

The association is large in the core model and survives several measurement and influence checks. The adjusted comparison is materially smaller and imprecise. Its strength depends on the specification.

Legal origin

The conditional differences are imprecise whether English common law is compared with all documented other origins or with named civil-code families. Classifications and geography shape the sample.

For a bank, the results suggest which inputs would be worth measuring directly when evaluating recovery and underwriting: recovery times, collateral enforceability, application rates and reasons for rejection. For policymakers and business associations, the negative core bribery association helps identify public transactions to study alongside application and financing outcomes. The study cannot rank the return on court reform against the return on anti-bribery policy. Establishing those returns would require linked outcomes and a design that isolates institutional changes from simultaneous differences in income, financial markets and firms’ choices.

10.1 Check your understanding

Why can a significantly negative bribery slope coexist with an inconclusive comparison to court doubt?

The individual test uses one slope and its variance. The direct comparison uses the two scaled slopes and their covariance. An interval for their difference can include zero even if one individual interval excludes zero.

Why repeat the core equation on the legal-origin sample?

Adding the dummy also removes observations with unavailable classification. The fixed-sample refit lets us see how the model changes when we add the dummy, given the restriction to the classified sample.

Would reordering the economies change the finance conclusion?

It changes which residual pairs are adjacent for Durbin–Watson. It leaves the OLS coefficients and row-specific fitted values the same. Dependence across regions warrants different checks from a time-series ordering.

Does a large in-sample R2R^2 settle whether a model is suitable for policy?

Fit describes how well the regressors account for variation in the observed outcome. A regressor may improve fit because it reflects an outcome of the same lending process. Policy interpretation also requires a credible design and a well-defined comparison.

The notebook uses the same data, model functions and estimates as the paper and the PDF appendix. Its visible examples recalculate key quantities and check that they agree with the pipeline. To regenerate the notebook from the repository root, run Rscript --vanilla scripts/notebook.R. With the R packages on your library path, the equivalent in the RStudio console is rmarkdown::render("notebook/notebook.Rmd"). The HTML code menu can show or hide every chunk and download the embedded R Markdown source. A full rerun uses the files in the repository.

# Analysis stages are sourced in order by scripts/build.R.

                 "02_models.R" = "OLS fits, HC3 tests and contrasts",

                 "04_sensitivity.R" = "Alternative specifications and fractional response",
                 "05_court_comparisons.R" = "Named country examples, court confidence and repeat-wave comparisons")
tab(data.frame(Stage = names(stage_notes), Purpose = unname(stage_notes)),
    "Analysis stages used in this notebook")
